title: Stochastic Pauli-path simulator for large-scale quantum optimization
authors: Kaining Zhang, Xinbiao Wang, Kunsheng Li, Qixin Zhang, Yuxuan Du, Min-Hsiu Hsieh, Dacheng Tao
abstract: Pauli-based simulators offer a promising route to large-scale classical simulation of quantum circuits in the low-magic regime. Yet their applicability remains largely limited to forward simulation, making them inadequate for optimization-driven quantum tasks such as variational state preparation and parameter initialization. Existing approaches either lack native support for gradient-based optimization or suffer from severe gradient bias. Here we propose the stochastic Pauli-path simulator (SPPS), a computational framework for large-scale quantum optimization that enables unbiased stochastic gradient estimation via Pauli-path sampling across optimization iterations. Our theoretical analysis shows that the proposed simulator yields unbiased gradient estimates and admits provable convergence guarantees. We systematically evaluate our proposal, including quantum eigensolver benchmarks with up to 100 qubits and quantum neural network benchmarks with up to 40 qubits. Across these tasks, SPPS faithfully tracks optimization dynamics, converges within minutes, and broadens the role of Pauli-based simulation from forward estimation to large-scale quantum optimization.
summary: This paper introduces the Stochastic Pauli-path Simulator (SPPS), a novel computational framework designed to enable large-scale classical simulation of quantum circuits used in optimization. By using path sampling and automatic differentiation, SPPS provides unbiased stochastic gradient estimates necessary for variational quantum algorithms. This advances the utility of Pauli-based methods beyond simple forward state estimation into practical quantum optimization.
main_problem: Developing a classical simulation method for large-scale quantum optimization tasks that can provide unbiased stochastic gradient estimates across optimization iterations.
main_result: The proposed Stochastic Pauli-path Simulator (SPPS) yields unbiased gradient estimates with provable convergence guarantees, successfully extending Pauli-based simulation from simple forward estimation to complex, large-scale quantum optimization.
method: SPPS uses path sampling across the full Pauli-path space during Heisenberg evolution and employs importance reweighting combined with Path Automatic Differentiation (PAD) to derive unbiased stochastic gradient estimators for variational quantum algorithms.

Theoretical sections provide convergence guarantees for Gradient Descent using these stochastic estimators. Finally, extensive benchmarks validate SPPS on VQE and state preparation tasks.
why_interesting: The development of scalable, gradient-aware classical simulators is crucial for benchmarking near-term quantum hardware performance in optimization regimes, providing a vital tool for theoretical study of NISQ algorithms.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Stochastic Pauli-path simulator for gradient estimation. (a) Overview of the SPPS framework. SPPS samples propagation paths from the full path space and combines them into unbiased estimators of both expectation values and gradients. The sampled paths are generated independently and can therefore be evaluated in parallel. (b) Core algorithm of SPPS. A group of sampled paths is first converted into an unbiased estimator of the target expectation value by importance reweighting. The same path-sampling mechanism is then coupled with path automatic differentiation to obtain unbiased stochastic gradient estimators.

FIG. 2. Biased optimization trajectories of Tb-PBS methods. Subplots (a), (b), and (c) show the energy error ϵ0 versus the optimization step t of pre-training VQE for the 15-qubit TFIM, which are simulated by using CT-, WT-, and FT-PBS with different truncation thresholds τ, γ, and ν, respectively. The physical meanings of these thresholds are given in Sec. III. The dashed curve denotes the exact GD baseline obtained using PennyLane.

FIG. 3. Performance of different PBS methods for pre-training VQE on the TFIM. (a) Energy error ϵ0 versus optimization step t for SPPS-driven GD and exact GD on the 15-qubit TFIM with different learning rates. (b) Final energy error ϵ0 versus optimization runtime for SPPS and three Tb-PBS methods on the 15-qubit TFIM with different thresholds. (c,d) Final energy error and optimization runtime for system sizes from 20 to 100 qubits. Error bars indicate the standard deviation over 10 independent runs.

FIG. 4. Performance of different PBS methods for pre-training QNN on the 40-QML task. (a,b) Training MSE and test R2 score versus optimization step t for SPPS, CT-, FT-, and WT-PBS, respectively. (c) Optimization runtime of the four methods. We use δ = 2−1 for SPPS, τ = 2−8 for CT, ν = 5 for FT, and γ = 2 for WT. Error bars show the standard deviation over 5 independent runs.

FIG. 5. SPPS versus tensor-network simulation on large-qubit VQE pre-training. We compare SPPS and a tensor-network baseline on the L = 6 TFIM VQE benchmark with n ∈{20, 40, 60, 80, 100} qubits. Figures (a) and (b) report the final normalized energy error ϵ0 and the optimization runtime, respectively. Error bars indicate the standard deviation over 10 independent runs.
